lessons.title: Mashing maize and sorghum with local malted grains
lessons.body: To make a good mash from maize or sorghum, you need to gelatinize the starch first. Crack 5 kg of maize or sorghum into a coarse grit using a hammer mill or a clean mortar and pestle. In a large pot, bring 20 liters of water to a boil. Slowly add the cracked grain while stirring to avoid lumps. Cook for 45â60 minutes until you get a thick porridge. This breaks down the starch so enzymes can reach it. Let the porridge cool to 65â68Â°C. If you don't have a thermometer, drip a little on your wristâit should feel very hot but not scalding. Now add your malted grain. You can malt your own sorghum or maize: soak grain for 24 hours, spread it in a thin layer, keep it damp, and let it sprout for 3â5 days until the sprouts are 1â2 cm. Then dry and crush it. Use 1 kg of malted grain for every 5 kg of unmalted grain. Stir the malt into the porridge and hold at 65Â°C for 1â2 hours. The enzymes in the malt convert starch to sugar. Test with iodine: a drop of mash on a white plate with a drop of iodine should not turn blue-black; if it does, keep mashing longer. After conversion, cool the mash to 30Â°C, add yeast, and ferment for 3â5 days. This mash can be distilled in a pot still. For sorghum, you may need to add a commercial enzyme or use more malt because sorghum starch is harder to gelatinize. Always use clean water and sanitize your tools to avoid spoilage.

lessons.title: Using cassava (garri) for a smooth, gluten-free spirit
lessons.body: Cassava, especially in the form of garri, is a great raw material for a gluten-free spirit. Garri is already partially gelatinized and dried, so it's easier to work with than raw cassava. Start with 5 kg of fine garri (white or yellow). In a large pot, mix the garri with 20 liters of water to form a smooth slurry. Heat the mixture to 75â80Â°C while stirring constantly. Do not boil vigorously; you want to gelatinize the starch without burning. Hold at that temperature for 20 minutes. The mixture will thicken. Now cool it to 65Â°C. Add 1 kg of crushed malted grain (barley, sorghum, or maize) or 5 ml of commercial alpha-amylase enzyme. Stir well and keep at 65Â°C for 1â2 hours. The enzymes will break down the starch into fermentable sugars. Check conversion with an iodine test: if it turns blue-black, continue mashing. Once converted, cool to 30Â°C and add yeast. Ferment for 4â6 days. Cassava mash can foam a lot, so leave headspace in your fermenter. After fermentation, distill in a pot still. Discard the first 50 ml of distillate (foreshots) as they contain methanol. Collect the middle run (heart) until the alcohol strength drops below 20% ABV. Cassava spirit is smooth and slightly sweet. Note: raw cassava contains cyanogenic compounds, but garri processing removes most of them. Still, always use food-grade garri and avoid bitter varieties. This method yields about 1.5â2 liters of 40% spirit per 5 kg of garri, depending on efficiency.

lessons.title: Extracting juice from sugarcane for rum-style spirits
lessons.body: Sugarcane is the classic raw material for rum. To extract juice, you need a cane crusher or a strong press. If you don't have a crusher, you can chop the cane into small pieces and pound it in a wooden mortar, then squeeze the pulp through a clean cloth. A more efficient way is to use a manual sugarcane juicer, which can be bought or rented in many African markets. For a small batch, take 20 kg of fresh sugarcane. Remove the leaves and cut the stalks into 30 cm lengths. Pass them through the crusher, collecting the juice in a clean bucket. You should get about 10â12 liters of juice. Strain the juice through a cloth to remove bits of bagasse. Now measure the sugar content with a refractometer or a hydrometer. You want a Brix reading of 12â18%. If it's higher, add clean water; if lower, add a little sugar. Adjust the pH to 4.5â5.0 using lemon juice or citric acid. Boil the juice for 10 minutes to sterilize it, then cool to 30Â°C. Add yeast (1 g per liter) and ferment for 3â5 days. The juice will bubble and then settle. Once fermentation stops, distill in a pot still. Rum gets much of its flavor from the cane juice and from aging. For a white rum, distill twice and filter through charcoal. For a golden rum, age in charred oak chips for a few weeks. You can also use molasses, a byproduct of sugar production, which is cheaper and gives a darker rum. But fresh cane juice gives a more aromatic spirit. Always clean your equipment to avoid bacterial contamination.

lessons.title: Preparing palm sap for distillation (toddy)
lessons.body: Palm sap, also called toddy, is a traditional African beverage that can be distilled into a strong spirit. You can tap sap from oil palm or raffia palm. The sap is collected from the inflorescence (flower stalk) before it opens. A tapper cuts the tip of the stalk and ties a calabash or plastic container to collect the dripping sap. This is usually done early morning and evening. Fresh sap is sweet and ferments quickly. To prepare it for distillation, you need to ferment it. If you want a consistent product, you can pasteurize the sap first: heat it to 70Â°C for 10 minutes to kill wild yeasts, then cool and add a known yeast strain. But traditional toddy is often left to ferment naturally for 1â2 days. The sap contains 10â15% sugar. It will ferment to about 5â8% alcohol. For distillation, you need at least 5 liters of fermented sap. Distill in a pot still. Discard the first 50 ml (foreshots) and collect the heart until the distillate drops below 20% ABV. The result is a clear, strong spirit, often called

. In some countries, it's illegal to distill toddy without a license, so check local laws. Also, palm sap can contain bacteria that produce off-flavors, so keep everything clean. If you want a smoother spirit, distill twice. You can also add a little sugar to the sap before fermentation to increase yield. But be careful: too much sugar can stress the yeast. A good yield is about 1 liter of 40% spirit from 10 liters of sap.

lessons.title: Enzymatic conversion with termite hill enzymes or commercial alpha-amylase
lessons.body: Enzymes are the key to breaking starch into sugar. In many African communities, termite hills are a source of natural enzymes. The termite hill material contains bacteria and fungi that produce amylase. To use it, collect dry, fresh termite hill soil (about 1 kg). Mix it with 5 liters of warm water (60Â°C) and let it steep for 2 hours. Strain the liquid through a cloth. This liquid contains enzymes. Add this to your cooled mash (65Â°C) and stir. However, termite hill enzymes are less predictable than commercial ones. For reliable results, use commercial alpha-amylase. It's sold as a liquid or powder in brewing shops or online. Dosage: 1 ml of liquid alpha-amylase per 10 kg of grain, or 1 g of powder per 10 kg. Add it when the mash is at 65â70Â°C. For glucoamylase (which breaks down dextrins to glucose), add it at 60Â°C after alpha-amylase. Always follow the manufacturer's instructions. You can also use malted grain as an enzyme source, as described in Lesson 1. To test enzyme activity, do an iodine test. If the mash turns blue-black, enzymes are still needed. If it stays brownish, conversion is complete. Remember that enzymes are proteins and can be denatured by high heat. So never add them to boiling mash. Also, adjust pH to 5.0â5.5 for best activity. If using termite hill enzymes, you may need to add more or combine with a little malt. Commercial enzymes are more expensive but give consistent yields. For a small distillery, it's worth investing in a bottle of alpha-amylase and glucoamylase.

lessons.title: Calculating mash efficiency and yield per kilogram of grain
lessons.body: Mash efficiency tells you how much sugar you actually extracted from the grain compared to the maximum possible. To calculate it, you need to measure the specific gravity (SG) of your mash before fermentation. Use a hydrometer. For example, if you mashed 5 kg of maize, the theoretical maximum extract is about 80% of the grain's weight as sugar. Maize is about 70% starch, and each kg of starch yields 1.11 kg of sugar. So 5 kg maize gives 5 * 0.70 * 1.11 = 3.885 kg of sugar. If you dissolve that in 20 liters of water, the total volume is about 23 liters (since sugar adds volume). The SG would be about 1.065 (using the formula: SG = 1 + (sugar in kg / (volume in L * 0.004))). But in reality, you might get SG 1.050. Your efficiency is (actual sugar / theoretical sugar) * 100. Actual sugar = (SG - 1) * volume * 1000 / 4. For SG 1.050 and 23 L, actual sugar = 0.050 * 23 * 1000 / 4 = 287.5 g? Wait, that's not right. The correct formula: sugar (g/L) = (SG - 1) * 1000 * 2.5? Actually, the extract in points per gallon (PPG) is common. But for simplicity, use a refractometer or hydrometer chart. A simpler method: after fermentation, measure the alcohol by volume (ABV) with a hydrometer or by distillation. Each kg of sugar yields about 0.51 kg of ethanol. So if you got 3 kg of sugar, you get 1.53 kg ethanol, which is about 1.94 liters of pure alcohol. That's about 4.85 liters of 40% spirit. So yield per kg of grain: for 5 kg maize, you might get 4 liters of 40% spirit. That's 0.8 L per kg. If you get less, your efficiency is low. To improve, grind finer, cook longer, use more enzymes, and control pH. Keep records of grain weight, water volume, SG, and final spirit volume. This helps you calculate cost and profit. For cassava, yield is similar but depends on starch content. For sugarcane, yield is based on sugar content of juice. Always aim for at least 70% efficiency.

quiz.q: What is the first step in mashing maize or sorghum?
options: B) Gelatinize the starch by cooking
quiz.explanation: Cooking gelatinizes the starch so enzymes can convert it to sugar.

quiz.q: How much malted grain should you add per 5 kg of unmalted grain?
quiz.explanation: A ratio of 1 kg malt to 5 kg unmalted grain provides enough enzymes for conversion.

quiz.q: What temperature should the mash be held at during enzymatic conversion?
quiz.explanation: Enzymes work best at 65â68Â°C; higher temperatures denature them.

quiz.q: What does an iodine test showing blue-black indicate?
quiz.explanation: Blue-black means starch remains; continue mashing until it turns brownish.

quiz.q: Why is garri preferred over raw cassava for making spirits?
options: B) It is already partially gelatinized and has less cyanide
quiz.explanation: Garri processing removes most cyanogenic compounds and pre-gelatinizes starch.

quiz.q: What temperature should you hold the cassava mash during enzymatic conversion?
quiz.explanation: 65Â°C is optimal for alpha-amylase activity.

quiz.q: How long should you ferment cassava mash?
quiz.explanation: 4â6 days allows complete fermentation at 30Â°C.

quiz.q: What should you discard during distillation to avoid methanol?
quiz.explanation: Foreshots contain methanol and other undesirable compounds.

quiz.q: What is the typical yield of 40% spirit from 5 kg of garri?
quiz.explanation: With good efficiency, 5 kg garri yields about 1.5â2 liters of 40% spirit.

quiz.q: What tool is used to extract juice from sugarcane?
options: B) A cane crusher or press
D) A mortar and pestle only
quiz.explanation: A cane crusher efficiently extracts juice from sugarcane.

quiz.q: What Brix reading is ideal for sugarcane juice before fermentation?
quiz.explanation: 12â18% sugar content gives good fermentation and yield.

quiz.q: Why should you boil sugarcane juice before fermentation?
options: B) To sterilize and kill wild microbes
quiz.explanation: Boiling sterilizes the juice, preventing unwanted bacteria from spoiling fermentation.

quiz.q: What pH range is recommended for sugarcane juice fermentation?
quiz.explanation: pH 4.5â5.0 is optimal for yeast and inhibits bacteria.

quiz.q: What is palm sap also known as?
quiz.explanation: Palm sap collected for fermentation is commonly called toddy.

quiz.q: How long does natural fermentation of palm sap typically take?
quiz.explanation: Wild yeasts ferment palm sap within 1â2 days.

quiz.q: Why is it important to check local laws before distilling palm toddy?
options: B) Distillation may require a license
D) It is only for export
quiz.explanation: Many countries regulate distillation of alcohol, including toddy.

quiz.q: What is a potential source of natural enzymes in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Termite hill material contains microbes that produce amylase enzymes.

quiz.q: How should termite hill enzymes be prepared for use?
options: B) Steep in warm water and strain
C) Add directly as dry powder
quiz.explanation: Steeping in warm water extracts the enzymes, which are then strained and added to mash.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dosage of liquid alpha-amylase per 10 kg of grain?
quiz.explanation: 1 ml of liquid alpha-amylase is typical for 10 kg of grain.

quiz.q: At what temperature should glucoamylase be added?
quiz.explanation: Glucoamylase works best at around 60Â°C.

quiz.q: Why should enzymes never be added to boiling mash?
options: B) They are denatured by high heat
quiz.explanation: High heat denatures enzymes, making them inactive.

quiz.q: What is the optimal pH for enzyme activity in mash?
quiz.explanation: Most amylase enzymes work best at pH 5.0â5.5.

quiz.q: What does mash efficiency measure?
options: B) How much sugar is extracted from grain compared to theoretical maximum
C) How much alcohol is in the final spirit
D) How clear the mash is
quiz.explanation: Efficiency is the percentage of theoretical sugar actually extracted.

quiz.q: What is the theoretical sugar yield from 1 kg of starch?
quiz.explanation: Each kg of starch hydrolyzes to about 1.11 kg of sugar.

quiz.q: How much ethanol is produced from 1 kg of sugar?
quiz.explanation: Yeast converts 1 kg sugar to about 0.51 kg ethanol.

quiz.q: If you get 4 liters of 40% spirit from 5 kg of maize, what is the yield per kg?
quiz.explanation: 4 liters / 5 kg = 0.8 liters per kg.

quiz.q: What can you do to improve mash efficiency?
options: A) Grind finer and cook longer
quiz.explanation: Finer grind and longer cooking increase starch availability.

quiz.q: What is the minimum efficiency you should aim for?
quiz.explanation: Aim for at least 70% efficiency for good profitability.

quiz.q: What is the main sugar in sugarcane juice?
quiz.explanation: Sucrose is the primary sugar in sugarcane juice.

quiz.q: What is the typical alcohol content of fermented palm sap?
quiz.explanation: Natural fermentation of palm sap yields about 5â8% alcohol.
